title: As-Sami', the All-Hearing
hookLine: the All-Hearing, who hears every whisper
tomorrow: if God is always watching, is that a threat or a comfort?

lines: A SURAH NAMED FOR AN ARGUMENT.
cards: Voice memos you never sent. A version text that says everything, sitting unsent since last night. Most of what people say never reaches anyone.
So here's an odd detail. One surah of the Qur'an is named for an argument. Al-Mujadilah: she who disputes.
Its very first word is a verb, and the verb is heard. Yesterday's question was why a surah would be named for a woman arguing.
The answer starts in a small room, with a woman pleading about her marriage, and someone sitting in the corner who can't make out all her words.

teach.b: Tradition names her Khawlah. Her husband had sworn an old oath that cut her off as a wife, and she came to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to plead her case, again and again.
Then the surah opens, in Pickthall's words: "Allah hath heard the saying of her that disputeth with thee." Her complaint goes into scripture, and the verses after it undo that oath's hold.

Here's the part to tell a friend tonight. In a hadith, Aisha says she was in the same room, and she could not hear some of what the woman said. Glory to the one whose hearing takes in every voice, she said.

teach.h: AISHA, A FEW FEET AWAY, MISSED IT.
teach.b: The person a few feet away missed it. The verse says Allah heard it all. That's As-Sami', the All-Hearing.
Not a speaker turned up loud.
In another hadith, when people were shouting their praise on a journey, the Prophet told them to go easy on themselves: you aren't calling on someone deaf or far away. So the puzzle solves itself.
The surah carries her name because she argued, and because her argument was heard. A whisper reaches. A complaint brought to Him is not a lack of faith; it's the opening line of a surah.

how: Muslims make du'a aloud or in a whisper, in Arabic or any language, at any time; the Qur'an's Surah al-Mujadilah opens with Allah hearing a woman's complaint.

o: the one who only hears prayers in Arabic
the one who hears the loudest voice first
the All-Hearing, who hears even a whisper

games.q: who heard what — tap the pairs.
p: in the room, missed some words
the one you call on, the Prophet said

s: Allah hears a prayer best when it's said loudly
the Prophet told shouting travelers to go easy: you aren't calling someone deaf or far away.
Aisha was in the same room and couldn't hear all of it
she said so in a hadith, and praised the one whose hearing takes in every voice.
bringing a complaint to God shows weak faith
a woman's complaint is the opening line of Surah al-Mujadilah.

games.q: your cousin's mosque friend tells her, 'don't ask God about your parents' fight. complaining to Him is ungrateful.' she asks you. what does Al-Mujadilah say?
o: he's right; keep problems to yourself and only give thanks.
bring it to Him; a woman's complaint opens a whole surah.
only complain out loud, in Arabic, so it's a proper du'a.
games.why: "Allah hath heard the saying of her that disputeth with thee." her plea went into scripture, and the verses after it changed her situation.

practice: Bring your voice down to almost nothing, lips barely moving. If you pray, whisper a du'a in your own words about the thing you haven't told anyone.
Or simply whisper that thing once, into the quiet, and let the sit hold the silence after it.

wordCard.voice: As-Sami'. The All-Hearing, who caught every word of a complaint that the person in the corner missed.

orig.note: Arabic: the All-Hearing. Surah al-Mujadilah opens with its verb: heard.

carryVoice: The line to keep: heard, every whisper, even the ones that never reach a phone. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: Allah hath heard the saying of her that disputeth with thee

sources.ref: Qur'an 58:2–4 (the ruling on the husband's oath)
Sunan Ibn Majah 188; Sunan an-Nasa'i 3460 (Aisha: blessed is He whose hearing takes in all voices; she could not hear some of what the woman said)
